prompt: I teach grade 6 science. Make me an interactive figure for tomorrow's lesson on why summer is hotter than winter. I've got about 10 minutes before my next class.
summary: I built a page where a 1 m wide noon sunbeam hits the ground in New York or Melbourne for any month. In summer it lands on a small, bright patch; in winter the low sun spreads it over a wide, dim patch, and there are fewer hours of daylight. A text box under the controls shows the sum (e.g. 100 ÷ 2.29 = 44 units of sunlight per metre), and a small graph shows the noon sun's height through the year. A switch turns Earth's tilt off and the seasons disappear. The challenge has students find New York's lowest noon sun (December) and notice Earth is nearer the sun then, not farther. I checked it with the month slider at both ends, in December, on a phone-width screen and in dark mode. Phone labels are small, and in dark mode the night part of the daylight bar is hard to see; the default light theme is fine.

rungs_skipped: None skipped. One small thing: the June and December markers use mid-month, about a week before the actual longest and shortest days.
